text:
customer-olivia: Hi all — after migrating some services to use an interface endpoint (PrivateLink) for Redwood, our requests intermittently 504 / gateway timeout only when we go via the endpoint. Direct internet path to the same API works fine. Happening across two AZs. Any pointers?

support-lee: thanks Olivia. Can you paste the minimal curl you used and a tcpdump showing the SYN/SYN-ACK/FIN? Also please include the endpoint id and SGs attached to the endpoint ENIs / target NLB.

customer-olivia: endpoint vpce-0f123abc in us-west-2. curl below:
```
curl -v https://api.redwood.internal/v1/health --connect-to api.redwood.internal:443:10.2.5.12
* Connected to api.redwood.internal (10.2.5.12) port 443 (#0)
* TLS handshake completes
* HTTP/1.1 504 Gateway Timeout
```
We captured tcpdump on the app host:
```
11:22:33.100 IP 10.1.4.21.54321 > 10.2.5.12.443: Flags [S], seq 1
11:22:33.150 IP 10.2.5.12.443 > 10.1.4.21.54321: Flags [S.], seq 100, ack 2
11:22:33.200 IP 10.1.4.21.54321 > 10.2.5.12.443: Flags [.], ack 101
11:22:35.300 IP 10.1.4.21.54321 > 10.2.5.12.443: Flags [P.], seq 2:100, ack 101
11:22:45.999 (no response from backend)
```
So it looks like handshake completes but no application response.

infra-jamie: couple of quick checks:
- Are your app instances behind a NAT / is SNAT happening? If so, traffic source to the VPCE will be NAT IPs, check SGs.
- Run `aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters Name=attachment.instance-owner-id,Values=amazon-vpce` to list VPCE ENIs and their SGs.
- Also run `aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <tg-arn>` for the NLB target group behind our service. If targets are unhealthy at the NLB level you can see timeouts.

customer-olivia: we do SNAT via a NAT gateway for our private subnet (legacy setup). Here's the ENI list and SGs (redacted):
```
eni-0a2b3c attached to vpce-0f123abc SGs: sg-070aaa (vpce-sg)
```
And our app instances are in subnet that goes through nat-0b123 (so source IP becomes 3.120.45.9). Our vpce-sg inbound rules only allow 10.0.0.0/16 on 443.

eng-ash: that is likely the issue — if your traffic is SNATed to the NAT gateway public IP then the VPCE ENI sees a source IP outside the allowed SG range and drops it. The apparent handshake/ack could be from connection tracking quirks but the application-level packets are blocked or not attributed, leading to 504 from the NLB or client timeout. Two ways customers fix this:
1) Make requests to the VPCE without SNAT (route directly to the interface endpoint from the app subnet) so source IPs are the private instance IPs.
2) Expand the vpce-sg inbound to include the NAT gateway IP or the app-subnet CIDR (less ideal security-wise).

support-lee: can you confirm whether your subnet route table has a specific route for the VPCE ENI or whether the default route sends all outbound to the NAT? If the latter, you can add a more-specific route to the VPC CIDR for the endpoint ENI IP via local so it doesn't hit NAT.

customer-olivia: route table currently has 0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-0b123 and no specific routes for the vpce IPs. We tried adding a host route to 10.2.5.12/32 -> local but AWS console rejects host routes in VPC route table.

infra-jamie: correct, VPC route tables don't allow /32 to point at ENIs. Two realistic fixes then:
- Add a route to the remote prefix used by the endpoint (if Redwood gave a small CIDR used for service ENIs) pointing to local — but most interface endpoints are per-enis dynamic.
- Better: Arrange for your app subnet to not SNAT traffic destined for the Redwood FQDN. Use an HTTP proxy inside the VPC that binds to the instance IP (no SNAT) or configure iptables policy-based routing to send traffic directly to the VPCE ENI MAC (advanced).
- Or, loosening the vpce-sg to accept the NAT gateway IP range for this specific service while you transition.

customer-olivia: we don't want to loosen SGs broadly. Is there an AWS-recommended pattern to avoid SNAT for cross-VPC interface endpoints?

eng-ash: common patterns:
- Put the app in a subnet with no NAT and allow direct internet only via endpoints; you control egress via egress-only or firewall appliances.
- Use an instance or ENI-based proxy in the same subnet as the app that forwards to the endpoint without SNAT (so source preserved).
- Use AWS Transit Gateway IP routing rules to preserve source (but that can be complex).
Another practical short-term: add the NAT's elastic IP to vpce-sg inbound on 443 only for the Redwood endpoint. That buys time while you re-architect.

customer-olivia: ok we'll do the temporary NAT-EIP allow and then plan a proxy approach. Before that, one more question: how do we verify that target health at Redwood NLB isn't part of the issue?

support-lee: run `curl -v --resolve api.redwood.internal:443:10.2.5.12 https://api.redwood.internal/health` from an instance that is NOT SNATed (e.g., a bastion in same subnet without NAT) and confirm 200. Also share `aws elbv2 describe-target-health` output if you have TG-ARN. If targets are healthy you'll see "healthy" states.

customer-olivia: did the NAT EIP trick (added EIP 3.120.45.9 to vpce-sg) and retried: success — HTTP 200 and no 504s. We then scheduled to deploy an internal proxy next week.

sre-bot: Incident INC-2024-0810 created and auto-closed: "Interface endpoint requests SNATed by NAT -> SG drop -> 504s; mitigated by whitelisting NAT EIP; planned fix: proxy/no-SNAT architecture" :white_check_mark:

support-lee: summary for KB: root cause = SNATed source IPs hitting VPCE SGs that only accepted internal CIDR; remediation = avoid SNAT for endpoint-bound traffic or update SGs temporarily; prevention = add VPCE onboarding checklist to verify endpoint SG inbound rules and NAT/SNAT interactions.

customer-olivia: thanks everyone, appreciate the clear next steps. We'll follow up when proxy is live and ask for a quick smoke test.

infra-jamie: happy to run the synthetic test after your deploy. Logged a short runbook with the tcpdump/curl checks we used.
